claims.text: Rapid quenching of FeCoNiTi produces a dual-phase microstructure containing an FCC matrix and C14 Laves precipitates.
The FCC matrix in the dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy is ferromagnetic.
Coexistence with the C14 Laves phase fundamentally alters the magnetic ground state of the FCC FeCoNiTi matrix.
Fe, Co, and Ni moments couple antiferromagnetically to non-magnetic or weakly magnetic Ti atoms at FCC/C14 interfaces.
Interfacial Ti induces local antiparallel spin alignment or spin frustration in neighboring Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
Ti-mediated antiferromagnetic coupling reduces the net magnetic moment and saturation magnetization.
The reduced volume fraction of ferromagnetic FCC material also suppresses the alloy's saturation magnetization.
C14 Laves precipitates act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
The distinct crystal structure and high FCC/C14 interfacial energy are responsible for strong domain-wall pinning.
The C14 phase is likely harder or more brittle than the FCC matrix, which helps it create strong pinning sites.
Domain-wall pinning by the C14 phase raises coercivity significantly above 100 Oe and could produce approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Dual-phase FeCoNiTi will have lower saturation magnetization than single-phase FCC FeCoNi because of Ti dilution and antiferromagnetic coupling.
The hysteresis loop of dual-phase FeCoNiTi will have a squareness ratio indicative of strong domain-wall pinning.
Single-phase FCC Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient and they lack pinning centers.
Antiferromagnetic-coupling concepts are transferred from Cr-containing high-entropy alloys.
The effectiveness of C14 pinning depends on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Quenching rate can change the size, distribution, and volume fraction of the Laves phase.
A DFT comparison of FCC configurations with and without Ti neighbors can test the spin-resolved density of states at the Fermi level.
Comparing single-phase FCC, dual-phase FCC+C14, and C14-dominant alloys can isolate the phase-specific magnetic contribution.
Comparable coercivity above 100 Oe in single-phase and dual-phase FeCoNiTi would falsify the claim that C14 pinning is the primary cause of high coercivity.
